passage:
Sunday night. Today I closed the app. Turned off the servers, sent the last email to users, and hugged Ankita at the doorway. It hurt more than I expected. Then, before the feeling could settle, I opened a notebook and wrote two pages headed What I learned. About the market: people wanted a cheap, simple tool, not our long list of features. About us: we never spoke openly when the numbers dropped, and we hired before we knew the need. I underlined three lessons. Ankita is going to help with the next idea: a small tool, one feature, and a check with real users in the first month. It is smaller. It feels lighter.

Uday

passage: In the small town of Palakkad, Naveen had spent two years on a farm-supplies delivery service. In March he finally shut it down. His friend Santosh found him on the veranda that evening with a school notebook. "Writing your will?" Santosh joked. Naveen smiled tiredly. "Writing what went wrong, before I forget." He read out his list: farmers wanted credit, not delivery; he'd hired cousins who didn't know logistics; he'd tried to cover six villages instead of two. Santosh whistled. "That's harsh on yourself." "It's useful," Naveen said. By June he had started again, smaller: a seed-testing stall in the weekly market, two villages only, one trained helper. The notebook sat on the stall's shelf.

qa.q: When did Naveen shut down the delivery service?
How did Naveen feel on the veranda that evening?
qa.a: He felt tired and a bit sad, smiling tiredly, but also determined to learn from what went wrong.

qa.q: What else could Naveen do before growing the new stall?
qa.a: Ask the farmers in the two villages every few weeks what they need, so he catches problems early this time.

qa.q: How does Santosh see Naveen's list?
qa.a: Santosh thinks Naveen is being harsh on himself, but seems to respect the honesty.
